1.pericope_label: Then Job answered and said, I know it is so of a truth: but how should man be just with God? If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one of a thousand. He is wise in heart, and mighty in strength: who hath hardened himself against him, and hath prospered?

schools.summary: Delitzsch fixes the assent to Bildad rather than to Eliphaz and reads it as irony, since what God does is always right because God does it; Ellicott takes man as the subject of the contending and offers two senses of one of a thousand.

Gill notes that Job ignores Bildad's harsh expressions and goes straight to the argument, gives both directions of the contending, and dwells on the infinite wisdom that sees every thought and action.

Clarke concedes the maxims while holding all his righteousness nothing beside immaculate holiness, and turns the thousand offences toward justification by faith; Wesley states the concession without heat.

Henry notices what Job lets pass, draws the rule that a truth is not to be resisted because an adversary urged it, and prefers a pious confession of sinfulness to the reading that makes the words a complaint of God's severity.

Gregory the Great makes the reply a lesson in how to argue, the good condemning what is amiss while adopting whatever was rightly said, and figures it as a tiller pulling the thorn while sparing the ear.

debates.question: What is Job conceding when he says I know it is so?

positions.position: A pious confession of man's sinfulness, his own included; the complaint reading is known and set aside
Irony: what God does is always right, because God does it
A flat personal acknowledgment that his own righteousness is nothing beside God's holiness
Either way: God with man, or man with God, a potsherd striving with its maker
Man with God, who cannot answer one question of a thousand

outliers.claim: Reads the opening as a rule of controversy: men in the heat of opposition reject even the truth from an unwelcome speaker, while the good sit as the most even umpires of an opponent's meaning.

themes: Then Job answered and said,
I know it is so of a truth: but how should man be just with God?
If he will contend with him, he cannot answer him one of a thousand.
He is wise in heart, and mighty in strength: who hath hardened himself against him, and hath prospered?

5.pericope_label: Which removeth the mountains, and they know not: which overturneth them in his anger. Which shaketh the earth out of her place, and the pillars thereof tremble. Which commandeth the sun, and it riseth not; and sealeth up the stars. Which alone spreadeth out the heavens, and treadeth upon the waves of the sea.

schools.summary: Delitzsch renders the passage as walking upon the heights of the sea and reports that Ewald, Hirzel and others construe the verb for spreading in the opposite sense, of letting the heavens down.

Gill keeps several senses open for the removing of mountains, produces a modern village swallowed by a landslip as evidence, rules earthquakes out of the shaking of the earth, gives five explanations of the sun that does not rise, and makes the spreading of the heavens a continuing act rather than a past one.

Clarke takes the removing of mountains for earthquakes and fastens on the suddenness, compresses the darkened sun into cloud or eclipse, and reads the sealing of the stars as a letter closed so that it cannot be read.

positions.position: Yes: mountains, valleys and whole islands carried off in an instant, with no warning
Not ordinary earthquakes, which are partial; the shaking belongs to the last day or to the flood

outliers.claim: Reads the spreading of the heavens as maintenance rather than creation: God continues to hold them spread so that they are not yet rolled up like a scroll, and does it alone, without angels or men.

themes: Which removeth the mountains, and they know not: which overturneth them in his anger.
Which shaketh the earth out of her place, and the pillars thereof tremble.
Which commandeth the sun, and it riseth not; and sealeth up the stars.
Which alone spreadeth out the heavens, and treadeth upon the waves of the sea.

9.pericope_label: Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south. Which doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number. Lo, he goeth by me, and I see him not: he passeth on also, but I perceive him not. Behold, he taketh away, who can hinder him? who will say unto him, What doest thou? If God will not withdraw his anger, the proud helpers do stoop under him.

schools.summary: Delitzsch renders the four constellations and takes God's working among men to be as invisible and irresistible as his working in nature, answerable to no one; Ellicott twice catches Job borrowing Eliphaz's own words, and calls the passage a depiction of unapproachable majesty whose truth is universally granted and constantly contravened in practice, while admitting that Rahab cannot be identified.

Gill identifies the first constellation against a rival rabbinic reading, sets out the degrees in which God is and is not seen, distinguishes what God never takes from his people from what he removes at pleasure, and separates the anger that does not last from the anger that never withdraws.

Clarke states the incomprehensibility in a line and the practical upshot in another, that it is of no use to contend with God; Wesley presses that Job repeats Eliphaz word for word in the original, deliberately, to show his agreement about the divine perfections.

debates.question: Who are the helpers of Rahab?

positions.position: Impossible to say whether Rahab is Egypt or a name for the fallen archangel; on the first there is probably an allusion to Pharaoh's overthrow, but the evidence is lacking
Rendered as stooping beneath him, with God not restraining his anger until it has done its work

outliers.claim: Points out that Job here quotes his opponent Eliphaz in the very same words of the original, and that the repetition is deliberate, to show how far he agrees with him.

themes: Which maketh Arcturus, Orion, and Pleiades, and the chambers of the south.
Which doeth great things past finding out; yea, and wonders without number.
Lo, he goeth by me, and I see him not: he passeth on also, but I perceive him not.
Behold, he taketh away, who can hinder him? who will say unto him, What doest thou?
If God will not withdraw his anger, the proud helpers do stoop under him.

14.pericope_label: How much less shall I answer him, and choose out my words to reason with him? Whom, though I were righteous, yet would I not answer, but I would make supplication to my judge. If I had called, and he had answered me; yet would I not believe that he had hearkened unto my voice. For he breaketh me with a tempest, and multiplieth my wounds without cause.

schools.summary: Gill measures the disproportion in Job's own terms and hears proportion rather than despair, distinguishes the righteousness of Job's cause and of his Redeemer from the legal and civil righteousness actually in question, gives two renderings of the calling and answering, and reports a rendering of the tempest as the burning wind of the east.

Clarke holds that a man clear of every charge would still not dare stand before immaculate holiness, and takes Job's hesitation as evidence confuting the friends' slander that he was presumptuous; Wesley has Job unable to credit an answer while the tokens of displeasure remain.
Henry sets aside the explanation that the despair springs from hard thoughts of God and traces it instead to Job's sense of his own imperfect righteousness and his cloudy apprehensions of God.

debates.question: Where does Job's despair of gaining God's favour come from?

positions.position: Not from hard thoughts of God but from the sense of his own imperfect righteousness
From the disproportion itself: a feeble creature cannot enter the lists with the wise in heart and mighty in strength

debates.question: How should the verse about calling and answering be read?

positions.position: As a question, if I cry will he answer me, on Broughton's rendering; or as past tense, though I have called and he has answered
Even an answer would not persuade him while the tokens of displeasure remain; he would take it for a pleasant dream

outliers.claim: Takes Job's doubt that God would notice so mean a being as sufficient refutation of the friends' charge that he was presumptuous and had no becoming notion of God's majesty.

themes: How much less shall I answer him, and choose out my words to reason with him?
Whom, though I were righteous, yet would I not answer, but I would make supplication to my judge.
If I had called, and he had answered me; yet would I not believe that he had hearkened unto my voice.
For he breaketh me with a tempest, and multiplieth my wounds without cause.

18.pericope_label: He will not suffer me to take my breath, but filleth me with bitterness. If I speak of strength, lo, he is strong: and if of judgment, who shall set me a time to plead? If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me: if I say, I am perfect, it shall also prove me perverse. Though I were perfect, yet would I not know my soul: I would despise my life.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the breath as recovery after complete exhaustion, calls the passage the most uncompromising acknowledgment of man's inability to stand in judgment while granting that its expression is enigmatic, and states the paradox that saying I am perfect is the act that proves a man perverse; Delitzsch sets out and rejects the usual reading of the innocence claim in favour of Job not knowing his own soul.
Gill reports the medical reading of the breathlessness and prefers the hot wind, takes the phrase as measuring how thick the blows came, and notes that the perfection supposed is only supposed.

Clarke observes that almost every term from here on is forensic and re-renders one clause as asking who would be a witness for me, and holds that God must have a reason he does not choose to explain; Wesley reduces the clause to pleading one's own innocency against God.

debates.question: What does not being suffered to take breath describe?

positions.position: Job's disease, an asthma or quinsy; or, preferably, the hot winds that take a man's breath away
Simply that there is no respite, the body suffering continually and the mind harassed
The action of breathing again after complete exhaustion

debates.question: Is the line an affirmation of innocence or a confession of self-ignorance?

positions.position: Usually taken as innocence flung out in scorn of his own life, which Delitzsch names four scholars for holding
Rather that he does not know his own soul: the contradiction has made him a stranger to himself

outliers.claim: Observes that almost all the terms of this part of the speech are forensic, taken from legal process and pleadings in the gate, and re-renders the clause about setting a time as asking who would be a witness for him.

themes: He will not suffer me to take my breath, but filleth me with bitterness.
If I speak of strength, lo, he is strong: and if of judgment, who shall set me a time to plead?
If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me: if I say, I am perfect, it shall also prove me perverse.
Though I were perfect, yet would I not know my soul: I would despise my life.

22.pericope_label: This is one thing, therefore I said it, He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked. If the scourge slay suddenly, he will laugh at the trial of the innocent. The earth is given into the hand of the wicked: he covereth the faces of the judges thereof; if not, where, and who is he?

schools.summary: Delitzsch renders the opening as a conclusion Job maintains rather than an observation, and takes the one thing to be that it is all one whether a man is innocent or not; Ellicott states without softening that God is pictured as laughing at the calamity of the innocent, and then places the argument as that of a man deliberately shutting faith out in order to confront his friends with the logic of facts.
Gill collects four renderings of the opening words, rules Satan out of the scourge, and refuses any inference from prosperity, since love and hatred are not to be known by these things.

Clarke states as plain experience that the worst men hold most of this world's goods, and offers two ways of relieving the hard clause, the idiom by which God is said to do what he permits, and Good's rendering which makes Injustice the agent.

debates.question: Who covers the faces of the judges?

positions.position: God, but by permission rather than action, so that he permits the eyes of judgment to be blinded
Not God at all: on Good's rendering the earth is given over to Injustice, and she hoodwinks the judges

debates.question: How is the picture of God laughing at the innocent to be taken?

positions.position: As Job's deliberate pessimism, the argument of a man shutting out faith to confront his friends with facts they cannot explain
As the one thing Job maintains, that innocence makes no difference to the outcome

outliers.claim: Draws the conclusion the book will need later: since the wicked hold the earth by God's own ordinance, the giving of worldly goods is no proof of goodness and their removal no evidence of wickedness.

themes: This is one thing, therefore I said it, He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked.
If the scourge slay suddenly, he will laugh at the trial of the innocent.
The earth is given into the hand of the wicked: he covereth the faces of the judges thereof; if not, where, and who is he?

25.pericope_label: Now my days are swifter than a post: they flee away, they see no good. They are passed away as the swift ships: as the eagle that hasteth to the prey. If I say, I will forget my complaint, I will leave off my heaviness, and comfort myself: I am afraid of all my sorrows, I know that thou wilt not hold me innocent.

schools.summary: Delitzsch supplies a fourth rendering of the swift vessels, ships of reeds, and renders the resolution as giving up dark looks for a cheerful face.

Gill takes the first comparison as a courier chosen for speed and, following Broughton, limits the days to the prosperous ones; he gives three renderings of the ships and lists what would have to be forgotten.

Clarke reports the Latin version that turns leaving off heaviness into changing the countenance, and parts from Coverdale and the Latin on the last clause, which means not that God does not favour an evildoer but that he will not acquit Job so as to remove his afflictions; Wesley finds the endeavour vain because fear outlasts suspended grief, and calls the closing words despair and impatience.
Henry marks the change of temperature, distinguishes complaining to God from complaining of God, and exempts the lament over lost prosperity as proper enough.

debates.question: What are the swift vessels Job compares his days to?

positions.position: The lightest-built ships, or oared vessels that go where one pleases, or pirate craft fast because unladen
Ships of reeds

debates.question: Is the complaint in this passage legitimate?

positions.position: The lament over lost prosperity is proper; what follows is complaining of God, which is not
The closing words proceed from despair and impatience

outliers.claim: Refuses the Latin and Coverdale reading of the last clause, which makes it a statement that God does not favour an evildoer, insisting the original means only that God will not acquit Job by taking his afflictions away.

themes: Now my days are swifter than a post: they flee away, they see no good.
They are passed away as the swift ships: as the eagle that hasteth to the prey.
If I say, I will forget my complaint, I will leave off my heaviness, and comfort myself:
I am afraid of all my sorrows, I know that thou wilt not hold me innocent.

29.pericope_label: If I be wicked, why then labour I in vain? If I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean; Yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch, and mine own clothes shall abhor me.

schools.summary: Delitzsch renders the washing with a second cleanser beside the snow water and follows the plunging into the pit with the clothes abhorring the man who wears them.

Gill gives two senses of the vain labour, notes that prayer is fitly called labour as a wrestling with God, explains snow water as an ancient wash that whitens the skin, denies that ablutions or moral duties or repentance can cleanse a man before God, and leaves the ditch open between the ditch of sin and the ditch of afflictions.
Clarke applies the vain labour to the resolution just abandoned, that it would be useless to counterfeit joy and leave off complaining.

debates.question: What is the ditch Job would be plunged into?

positions.position: Either the ditch of sin, in which he must appear exceedingly impure beside God's holiness, or the ditch of afflictions, present or still to come
A pit, followed by the man's own clothes abhorring him

outliers.claim: Denies that anything a man can do makes him clean before God - not the ceremonial washings that may have been in use in Job's time, which purify only the flesh, nor moral duties, nor even repentance.

themes: If I be wicked, why then labour I in vain?
If I wash myself with snow water, and make my hands never so clean;
Yet shalt thou plunge me in the ditch, and mine own clothes shall abhor me.

32.pericope_label: For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, and we should come together in judgment. Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both. Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me: Then would I speak, and not fear him; but it is not so with me.

schools.summary: Delitzsch's rendering keeps the gesture the English loses, an arbitrator who should lay his hand upon them both, and leaves the closing line where the chapter leaves it.

Gill explains the human members ascribed to God as spoken after the manner of men, quotes the observation that an umpire must be wiser and mightier than both parties, insists the rod to be removed is the rod of affliction and not the sceptre of government, and allows a devotional sense of the last verse before preferring the plainer one.

Clarke traces the English word daysman through the law to arbitration by consent, allows that the rod may be the sceptre and the scene a judgment seat too appalling to speak before, and preserves the Masoretic note on the enlarged letter; Wesley states the disparity in half a line.

debates.question: Is the rod Job asks to have removed the rod of affliction or the sceptre of rule?

positions.position: The rod of affliction; Job had no wish to be freed from God's government
Possibly the sceptre: God seated in majesty on the judgment seat, a sight that makes prayer impossible

outliers.claim: Preserves the Masoretic note that the word for his rod is written with an oversized letter standing for nine, marking the nine calamities Job asked God to remove.

themes: For he is not a man, as I am, that I should answer him, and we should come together in judgment.
Neither is there any daysman betwixt us, that might lay his hand upon us both.
Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me:
Then would I speak, and not fear him; but it is not so with me.
